name: Thematic Coding
title: Thematic Coding
answer: Thematic coding is the family of qualitative techniques for marking segments of text or talk with labels and then grouping those labels into broader themes. It is used on interview transcripts, focus group recordings, field notes, open survey answers, documents and case files, and it sits at the centre of qualitative analysis and mixed methods work. The unit of analysis is usually a passage rather than a whole document, so a single transcript can carry many codes and a single code can appear across many transcripts. The output is not a number but a structured account, typically a codebook, a set of themes with definitions, and quoted evidence for each. The site's library, which holds 12646 claims extracted from research works, is a large scale version of the same move, pulling short statements out of longer documents and labelling them.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on source material that has been transcribed, cleaned and de-identified, plus a place to store codes and their links back to the text. Many teams use a spreadsheet or a shared document for small studies, while larger projects use dedicated qualitative data analysis packages such as NVivo, ATLAS.ti, MAXQDA or Taguette. These tools handle coding, retrieval, memos, matrices and team permissions, and they keep an audit trail of who coded what and when. Audio and video need transcription first, and the transcript becomes the working object even when the original recording is kept for verification. Increasingly a language model sits alongside the package, suggesting candidate codes or summarising passages, with the human coder deciding what stays.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Most projects begin with familiarisation, reading or listening through the material before any labels are applied. Coding then proceeds in passes, often open coding first, where short descriptive labels are attached close to the data, followed by grouping into categories and then into themes. Deductive coding works the other way, starting from an existing framework or interview guide and mapping the data onto it, and many studies mix the two. Memos record the reasoning behind a code, constant comparison checks new passages against earlier ones, and the codebook is revised as definitions sharpen. When several coders are involved, teams calibrate on a shared sample, discuss disagreements and report agreement, and the process continues until new material stops producing new themes.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Transcripts carry personal data, so consent, confidentiality and data protection rules shape what can be collected, stored and quoted. Identifiers are usually removed or replaced before coding, and quotes are checked for details that could re-identify a participant even after names are gone. Provenance matters as much as the codes, which means keeping the codebook version, the date of each change, the coder's name and the link from every theme back to the passages that support it. When a language model is used, teams record which model, which version and which prompt produced a suggestion, and note what a human reviewed or changed. The common risks are overclaiming from a small or unrepresentative sample, treating frequency of a code as importance, and letting a tidy theme list hide cases that do not fit.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Language models are shifting the practical ceiling on how much text a team can code, which makes very large interview sets and open text survey responses more tractable than before. That scale brings a countervailing push for transparency, with shared codebooks, preregistered coding plans and clearer reporting of how much of the analysis was machine suggested. Mixed methods designs are drawing thematic codes into closer contact with quantitative variables, so a theme can be tested against survey measures rather than only illustrated by quotes. Tooling is likely to keep moving toward hybrid workflows, where a model drafts and a researcher adjudicates, and where the audit trail is expected to show both. The unresolved question is whether faster coding improves interpretation or simply produces more themes with less time spent thinking about them.
